tagline.text: October festival in Dumaguete that gathers every Negros Oriental town festival

location.label: Location
location.text: Dumaguete City, Negros Oriental (around the Lamberto Macias Sports and Cultural Complex, Freedom Park and Rizal Boulevard)

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: Mid to late October (yearly, about one week)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱3,000~9,000 (excluding flights from Manila; 1 night's lodging, meals and local transport, rough estimate per person)

children.text: The Buglasan Festival is the signature festival of Negros Oriental, held in Dumaguete for about a week every October. Called the "festival of festivals" because it brings together the celebrations of every city and town in the province, it features a showdown, street dancing, fireworks and pageants.

The Buglasan Festival is held every October in the provincial capital, Dumaguete City, by the province of Negros Oriental in the Visayas of the central Philippines. It is called the "festival of festivals" because the large and small town festivals of the province's cities and towns come together in one place, and events run for about a week in the streets, stadiums and parks. It honors the province's history and cultural diversity, and it also has a religious side, giving thanks to each town's patron saint.

The name goes back to Buglas, the old name of the island. Buglas is described as a word for the tall reed-like grass that once covered the island, and one explanation says the name "Buglas Insulis" appears on an old map drawn by Diego Lope Povedano in 1572. Accounts of when the festival began differ by source. One says it started in 1981 as a local event, and another says it began in the 1990s when all the towns agreed to unite as one community. Either way, it has continued as a festival shared by the whole province.

The dates change every year; some sources say the second week of October and others say the last week. In 2016 it opened on October 14 and ended on October 23, and in 2024 it ran from October 18 to 27. In 2016, a presidential proclamation made the opening day a special non-working day, which made it easy for residents to take part. The event is run by the provincial government, so check the Negros Oriental provincial government or Dumaguete City notices for this year's dates before you go.

For travelers, this festival is a good reason to visit Dumaguete. By day you can stroll the modest seaside city and enjoy local food, and in the evening you can enjoy the night shows and the food fair at Freedom Park. With nearly 25 cities and towns in the province taking part, it is also appealing to meet the character of each area at once. During festival week, however, lodging fills up early and traffic is controlled in some parts of the city, so plan early. Dumaguete is close to Sibulan Airport and the port, and its small center is easy to cover on foot, which makes it easy to fit other plans around the festival.

Contingents from each city and town march and dance down the roads in costumes and props based on their own town festivals. The street events have been reported on National Road and Real Street, and sometimes on Rizal Boulevard. Routes and times change every year, so check the on-site notices. Because each contingent draws on its own festival, costume colors and dance moves vary greatly even within the same province, so you can compare many local cultures at once.

A more formal contest held at the Lamberto Macias Sports and Cultural Complex. You can watch it more comfortably seated than at the street events, so it suits appreciating the choreography and costume details. Entry arrangements can change from year to year, so check.

Near the end of the festival, a fireworks contest between cities and towns runs over two nights. It is also a competition among participating areas, so the mood gets heated. The colors and arrangements are fun to watch, and many people stay until late in the evening. It is better to claim a spot early.

blocks.title: Buglasan King and Queen, Miss Negros Oriental

children.text: The pageants of festival week. In 2016 the Miss Negros Oriental pageant was held on October 16 at the Lamberto Macias Sports Center, and the organizers said they aimed to raise it to a standard fit for national-level competitions.

blocks.title: Freedom Park night shows and food fair

children.text: Freedom Park gets a large stage, food stalls and exhibit booths, with bands and concerts every night. A market sells local food and handicrafts, which makes it a good place to go in the evening.
Traditional music and dance, and art and handicraft exhibits, take place. There are corners that show each town's character, so you can sample the culture of the whole province bit by bit.
At the end of the festival a civic parade takes place, with delegations from each area marching through the streets. It is the most colorful moment, so it is a shame to miss.
Between events, try Dumaguete snacks such as silvanas (frozen buttercream cookies), budbud kabog (millet rice cake), suman and tempura fish cakes. Many street stalls open around Rizal Boulevard.

items.title: 2-day, 1-night course
items.subtitle: Stroll Dumaguete by day, Freedom Park by night

children.text: Arrive at Dumaguete-Sibulan Airport (DGT) from Manila or Cebu and drop your bags at your lodging. Rooms fill up early during festival week.
Enjoy lunch and snacks around Rizal Boulevard. You can also walk around Silliman University.
Watch the street dance procession around National Road, or the showdown at the Lamberto Macias complex.
Enjoy the food fair and night shows at Freedom Park.
On the second morning, visit a nearby sight (such as Casaroro Falls) or join the final events.
Head out in time for your flight or ferry home.

Some venues have roads in town controlled, so tell your tricycle driver where you are going and ask about detours. On the second morning you can buy silvanas as a souvenir at a bakery in town. They are frozen products and may melt on a long trip, so check the packaging.

items.title: Relaxed weekend course
items.subtitle: The festival together with the nearby sea

children.text: In the morning, do a same-day marine activity toward Dauin or Apo Island.
Return to town, rest and prepare for the evening events.
Head to Freedom Park and enjoy the food fair.
At the end of the festival, watch the fireworks.
If you do an island tour on an event day, your return may be late, so leave plenty of time for the evening events.
There are flights from Manila and Cebu to Dumaguete-Sibulan Airport (DGT). Routes and timetables change, so check with the airline.
The airport is about
3 km
from the city, and you can get to town by tricycle or taxi. Check fares on site.
Ferries and fast crafts run to Dumaguete from Cebu, Bohol and Siquijor. From Cebu the trip is described as roughly 4 to 5 hours; check schedules and fares with the shipping company.
From other cities on Negros island such as Bacolod, travel by bus or van.
Tricycles are the basic transport in Dumaguete. Fares depend on distance, so negotiate when you board.
You can walk to some venues, but traffic is controlled during the street events.

The Buglasan Festival is held in October. It ran October 14–23 in 2016, October 20–27 in 2019 and October 18–27 in 2024, so the dates shift a little every year. You cannot see an event of this scale at other times, so be sure to plan your visit from the latest notices.
October is near the end of the rainy season, but it can still rain. The street events may be rescheduled in the rain, so bring a raincoat. It is humid, but temperatures are relatively warm.

If seeing the festival is not your goal, the dry season from December to February gives steadier weather for Dumaguete and nearby dive sites. If you do come for the festival, be ready for rain and be sure to check the street event times in the local notices.

Dumaguete has a range of lodging, from resort-style hotels to mid-range hotels and budget chains. Places that have been featured include The Henry Resort with its garden and pool, Hotel Essencia in the city center, and Go Hotels near Robinsons Mall. Rooms go quickly during festival week, so book one to two months ahead. Facilities and rates vary by season, so check recent reviews.

Food is varied, as befits a seaside city. Dumaguete's signature silvanas are frozen cookies filled with buttercream, and near Rizal Boulevard you can find street food such as tempura (fried fish cakes) and balut. Budbud kabog is a millet cake steamed in banana leaves, and suman is a glutinous rice snack cooked in coconut milk. The Dumaguete take on Bicol Express and lechon kawali are also worth trying.

If you cannot find lodging, you can stay in a nearby coastal town such as Dauin or Sibulan and travel into the city. Check the transport home after the night events beforehand. Some restaurants in town stay open late, but queues get long during the festival, so adjust your meal time to an early or late dinner.
Check the Negros Oriental provincial government and Dumaguete City notices for this year's dates.
Book lodging, flights and ferry seats early, as they sell out during festival week.
The sun is strong at the street events, so bring a hat, sunscreen and water.
Freedom Park is crowded in the evening, so keep your belongings in front of you.
Bring cash and small change. Market stalls and tricycles are generally cash.
A walk along Rizal Boulevard is cool and pleasant around sunset.
Dumaguete is known as the "City of Gentle People." Respect its quiet, friendly atmosphere.
If you want to visit nearby Apo Island or Casaroro Falls too, set aside a separate day. Check travel times on site.
During the loud fireworks, keep children and pets away from the area.
October is the tail end of the rainy season, so rain and typhoons can affect it and the schedule can change.
Street event schedules can change with the weather, so check the notices.
Traffic in town is controlled and congested during festival week.
Watch for pickpockets at crowded night venues.
Check the hygiene of seafood and street food before you eat.
If you combine an island tour, your return may be late, so leave extra time.
Roads can be slippery in the rainy season, so watch your step when getting in and out of tricycles.
The provincial capital where the festival takes place, a compact city that blends a seaside promenade with a university district.
Dumaguete's seaside promenade, a good place for street food and sunsets in the evening.
An old university campus in the city center that you can look around on foot.
